summary: The investigation ended inconclusive. The reviewed top hypothesis (H2, shared-host resource exhaustion / IOPS throttling starving ledger-db, confidence 0.10) is well below the 0.50 support threshold: it is supported only by historical precedent (F5) and is contradicted by the observed metrics (F17 shows flat disk usage; F12/F16 show the load is a portfolio-service Seq Scan, not a storage event). The evidence strongly points to a different, non-ranked mechanism: portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployed at 08:56Z (F1) introduced an unindexed Seq Scan over the 48.2M-row trades table (F12/F15), which drove ledger-db CPU to ~95-96% and tripled active connections (F10), flooding the shared DB with multi-second queries (F9/F16) and causing collateral statement timeouts on order-service INSERTs (F8/F18). The reporter's autovacuum suspicion (H1) is rejected on timing and mechanism (F7, F14), and no lock/blocking evidence exists (F13). Because the reviewed ranking fixed H2 on top at 0.10, and the alternative explanation — while strongly evidenced — has not been formally ranked and still rests on unavailable host/IOPS telemetry, the honest outcome is inconclusive; immediate mitigation should focus on the 08:56Z portfolio-service change.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared-host resource exhaustion / IOPS throttling starves ledger-db (HIST-110 pattern)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: ledger-db's host or storage volume is starved of a shared resource (cloud volume burst credits exhausted -> IOPS throttle, or another tenant's workload) independent of any order-service or portfolio-service change, and the reported latency is the visible symptom of that infrastructure/resource degradation. HIST-110 (2026-01-15) recorded exactly this mechanism for the identical symptom set.

causal_chain.claim: Host/volume resource for ledger-db (IOPS burst credits or co-tenant load) is exhausted, throttling IO
ledger-db query execution slows for all callers, including order-service's INSERTs
order-service p99 exceeds 5s with statement timeouts (F5 historical precedent, HIST-110)

assumptions: an IOPS/burst-credit mechanism exists on this volume (no metric available to test)
infra changes in the window are unverified due to missing tools

ranked_hypotheses.title: DBA autovacuum scale-factor change on ledger-db degrades query latency (reporter's suspicion)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The 08:00Z change of autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor from 0.2 to 0.1 on ledger-db made autovacuum more aggressive, causing vacuum IO/lock competition (or bloat-driven plan/IO behaviour change) that slowed ledger-db queries, which order-service experienced as statement timeouts on INSERT INTO orders.

causal_chain.claim: ledger-db autovacuum scale factor changed 0.2 -> 0.1 at 08:00Z, only ledger-db config change in window (F2)
More aggressive autovacuum would run vacuums on trades, competing with query IO/CPU, degrading all callers of ledger-db
order-service INSERTs then slow and time out, giving p99 > 5s

assumptions: autovacuum could affect the trades table's IO/CPU enough to cause 5s+ timeouts
the change is global/per-table in a way that touches trades (target table unknown per gaps)
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Timing: the config change is at 08:00Z but the latency/CPU/slow-query step is at 08:56Z, a 56-minute quiet gap with steady ~143-167ms p99 in between (F7). Mechanism: autovacuum INFO logs show routine audit_log cycles at unchanged cadence before and after the change, with no vacuum on trades and no blocking (F14), and no lock/deadlock evidence exists (F13). Also the slow-query flood is all attributable to portfolio-service's new Seq Scan (F12, F16), which began at the deployment minute, not the config change.

ranked_hypotheses.title: A caller other than order-service creates lock contention / long transactions on ledger-db
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A service (e.g. settlement-service or payment-service) holds locks or long transactions on ledger-db, and the autovacuum change altered how readily those block; order-service INSERTs into orders are blocked and time out. This treats the autovacuum change as an enabling condition rather than the direct cause.

causal_chain.claim: Some other ledger-db caller opens long transactions / holds locks on rows order-service's INSERT path needs
order-service INSERT INTO orders waits on the lock and hits the statement timeout

assumptions: lock waits exist but were not logged (logging-omission caveat from gaps)
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F13: searches for 'lock' (08:50-10:59Z) and 'deadlock' (05:00-10:59Z) in ledger-db logs returned zero matches; the sole WARN pattern is portfolio-service's slow query. No blocking-chain evidence exists, and the observed signatures (CPU ~96%, connections tripling) are consistent with CPU contention, not lock waits.

facts.statement: Exactly one deployment occurred in the 2026-05-05T00:00Z-09:30Z window: portfolio-service v4.5.0 at 08:56:00Z (change: new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at, no migration). No order-service deployment occurred.
Exactly one config change was recorded: ledger-db autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor changed 0.2 to 0.1 at 08:00:00Z by dba-team; this was the only ledger-db config change through 10:59Z.
ledger-db is a shared postgres called directly by four services (order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service, settlement-service).
order-service latency_p99_ms stepped from steady ~143-167ms (08:00-08:52Z) to 1514.78ms avg (max 5607.8) in the 08:56Z bucket, then ~5000-5500ms through 10:00Z; the change was not gradual.

The first order-service ERROR (statement timeout on INSERT INTO orders) was at 09:00:42Z; 142 such ERRORs occurred in 08:00-10:00Z, all matching 'ledger-db: canceling statement due to statement timeout (INSERT INTO orders)'.
ledger-db slow_queries_per_min jumped in the 08:56Z bucket from ~0.8-1.3/min to avg 70.42 (max 139.68), then ~135-148/min thereafter.

ledger-db connections_active jumped in the 08:56Z bucket from ~60-64 to avg 127.45 (max 199.81), then ~185-197; cpu_pct rose from ~30% to 63.26% (max 96.36) in the same bucket and to ~95-96% from 09:00Z on.
portfolio-service latency_p99_ms showed the same step and was the worst hit: ~174-195ms through 08:52Z, then 3574.3 avg at 08:56Z and ~6800-7200ms through 10:00Z.

All 185 ledger-db slow-query WARN matches (first 08:58:38Z) are the same pattern issued by application_name=portfolio-service: 'SELECT * FROM trades WHERE account_id=$1 AND executed_at > $2 ORDER BY executed_at -- Seq Scan on trades (rows=48211907)'. No slow query in the window is attributed to order-service.

Ledger-db logs contain NO lock contention, blocking-chain or deadlock evidence in the incident window ('lock' search 08:50-10:59Z returned 0 matches; 'deadlock' search 05:00-10:59Z returned 0 matches).

Autovacuum activity was not anomalous or IO-heavy: ledger-db INFO logs show the routine 'autovacuum: processed table public.audit_log' cycle continuing at unchanged cadence before and after the 08:00Z config change, with no vacuum on trades and no long-running vacuum entry.

The trades Seq Scan onset is at the minute level: slow_queries_per_min was flat ~0.7-1.1/min through the 08:53Z bucket, then jumped to avg 47.34 in the 08:56Z bucket and ~137-146/min from 08:59Z on, matching the 08:56Z portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployment rather than the 08:00Z autovacuum change.

Disk saturation is absent: ledger-db disk_used_pct is essentially flat and slowly declining across 08:00-09:30Z (mean 71.03%), with no step at 08:56Z, indicating the bottleneck is CPU/query execution, not disk fill or an IO volume event.

Interpretation: the statement timeouts are a CPU-contention/collateral effect, not lock waits — the portfolio-service Seq Scan on the 48.2M-row trades table floods ledger-db with multi-second queries, saturating shared CPU so order-service INSERTs exceed their statement timeout; the 08:00Z autovacuum change is temporally separated (55+ min) from the 08:56Z load step.

Historical precedent HIST-110 (2026-01-15) matched the current symptom set most closely, with root cause cloud volume burst credits exhausted leading to IOPS throttling; HIST-111 (2025-05-22) shows ledger-db slow queries/high DB CPU caused by a new unindexed report query (bad_deployment).

assumptions: The reviewed ranking is fixed; H2 (shared-host resource exhaustion / IOPS throttling) remains the top-ranked hypothesis at 0.10 confidence but is below the support threshold, so this report does not promote the strongly-evidenced portfolio-service explanation into the formal ranking.

Determining the causal mechanism (CPU contention from a new unindexed Seq Scan) is treated as an interpretation drawn from verified observations (F12, F15, F16, F10, F18), not as a formally ranked hypothesis.

The statement timeouts on order-service INSERTs are assumed to be collateral of shared ledger-db CPU saturation rather than resource limits specific to order-service, based on the coincident step in all four series.
The absence of lock/deadlock evidence is assumed to reflect true absence of lock waits rather than logging omission, though the gaps note list logging omission as a possible explanation.

Portfolio-service's new query is assumed to be the load source for the slow-query flood because every slow-query WARN in the window carries application_name=portfolio-service, though we did not directly observe request volume for that endpoint.
The 4-minute metric bucket resolution is assumed adequate to bracket the onset to 08:56Z-09:00Z; finer timing is not established.

(demoted from facts: no verified observation backs it) The two in-window changes are close to the reported onset (09:10Z): the ledger-db autovacuum change at 08:00Z (70 min before) and the portfolio-service deployment at 08:56Z (14 min before), and portfolio-service shares ledger-db.

recommended_actions.action: Roll back or disable portfolio-service v4.5.0 (the 08:56Z deployment, change list: new query on trades filtered by account_id + executed_at), or gate the new holdings-API P&L query behind a feature flag, to remove the trades Seq Scan load from ledger-db.
recommended_actions.rationale: The slow-query flood begins in the same 08:56Z bucket as the deployment and consists entirely of this new Seq Scan (F12, F15, F16); removing the load is the most direct safe mitigation for the shared DB affecting all four callers.

recommended_actions.action: Add a temporary server-side guard (e.g., lower statement_timeout for the portfolio-service role, or shed/reject the holdings API request) to limit concurrent Seq Scan executions on ledger-db while the fix is prepared.
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents the 48.2M-row sequential scan from saturating shared CPU and continuing to cancel order-service INSERTs; the mechanism is CPU contention, not locking (F10, F13, F18).

recommended_actions.action: Avoid reverting the autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor change as the primary mitigation; if reverted, do it only as a test and verify no latency improvement to confirm it is not the cause.
recommended_actions.rationale: Autovacuum shows no anomalous/heavy activity (F14) and the timing gap (08:00Z change vs 08:56Z step) is 56 minutes with steady latency in between (F7); reverting it alone is unlikely to resolve the incident.

recommended_actions.action: Verify mitigation: confirm ledger-db cpu_pct and slow_queries_per_min return toward baseline and order-service p99 drops below 5s after the new query is removed; then add a supporting index on trades(account_id, executed_at) and re-enable the feature.
recommended_actions.rationale: Confirms causal mechanism and provides a durable fix; the query filters on account_id + executed_at with ORDER BY executed_at (F12).

recommended_actions.action: Instrument/deploy a query-level guardrail: CI or pre-deploy check flagging Seq Scans on large tables (trades rows=48211907), and alerting on per-application slow-query rate and shared-DB CPU saturation.
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents recurrence of an unindexed report query on a shared DB; HIST-111 records the same bad_deployment pattern (new unindexed report query causing ledger-db CPU/slow queries).

recommended_actions.action: Adopt DB-host/storage telemetry (IOPS, burst credits, wait events, pg_stat_activity/lock-wait counters) so that the residual H2 IOPS-throttling hypothesis can be directly tested in future incidents.
recommended_actions.rationale: No IOPS/burst-credit or wait-event metric exists, leaving H2 untestable; HIST-110 recorded exactly this mechanism for the same symptom set (F5), and the gaps note these data are unavailable.

data_gaps: Cannot state which ledger-db tables the autovacuum change applied to, nor whether other autovacuum parameters changed (config listing returned only one entry, no target-table field).
Feature-flag and non-DB infra changes in the window are unverified (no tool beyond get_deployments/get_config_changes).
No host/node-level or IOPS/burst-credit telemetry was available, so the H2 IOPS-throttling hypothesis cannot be directly tested; only ledger-db cpu_pct (peak ~96-98%) was observable.

ledger-db exposes no query_latency, lock_waits, statement_timeout_count, wait-event, pg_stat_activity or pg_locks metrics; statement-timeout evidence comes only indirectly from order-service ERROR logs.
Onset cannot be pinned below the 4-minute bucket size (bracketed to 08:56Z-09:00Z); the CPU step was not re-confirmed at 1-minute resolution due to tool-call budget exhaustion.
order-service error_rate curve, ledger-db disk_used_pct confirmation at finer resolution and replication_lag_ms were not retrieved before the budget was exhausted.
The exact blocking-chain/session breakdown cannot be produced: no per-session blocking telemetry exists, and the no-lock conclusion rests on absence of lock/deadlock log lines.

It cannot be fully excluded that the autovacuum scale-factor change affected trades-table bloat/vacuum behavior; no log line records the change's target table beyond routine public.audit_log processing.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that the portfolio-service slow-query flood and ledger-db CPU step precede the 08:56Z deployment (e.g., minute-resolution series showing onset at or before 08:00Z) would undermine the portfolio-service query as the driver.
Host/storage telemetry showing IOPS throttling, burst-credit exhaustion or a node-level saturation event at 08:56Z would support the top-ranked H2 (HIST-110 pattern) over CPU contention.
Log evidence of lock waits, blocking chains or deadlocks (e.g., pg_stat_activity or explicit lock log lines) would contradict F13 and reopen H3.
A measurable latency improvement immediately after reverting the autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor change, without removing the new portfolio-service query, would support H1.

Demonstration that the new trades query is served by an index or is not actually executing a Seq Scan (e.g., query plan without the 48.2M-row scan) would remove the primary load source and force re-evaluation.
Evidence that one of the other ledger-db callers (payment-service or settlement-service) also degraded before 08:56Z would point to a pre-existing shared-DB condition rather than the new deployment.

No vacuum-on-trades, no vacuum blocking, no long-running vacuum entry appears. This argues against autovacuum heavy-vacuum IO competition as the mechanism.

findings.statement: The trades Seq Scan onset at the minute level: slow_queries_per_min is flat ~0.7-1.1/min through the 08:53Z bucket (avg 1.06), then jumps to avg 47.34 (max 139.17) in the 08:56Z bucket and ~137-146/min from 08:59Z on. This matches the 08:56Z portfolio-service v4.5.0 deployment, i.e. the slow-query flood starts with/just after the new query going live, not at the 08:00Z autovacuum change.

Disk-related saturation is absent: ledger-db disk_used_pct is essentially flat and slowly declining across 08:00-09:30Z (avg ~70.7-71.8%, min 69.62, max 72.48, mean 71.03), with no step at 08:56Z. Combined with the CPU step, this indicates the bottleneck is CPU/query execution, not disk fill or an IO volume event.

Interpretation: the statement timeouts are a CPU-contention/collateral effect, not lock waits — the new portfolio-service Seq Scan on the 48.2M-row trades table floods ledger-db with multi-second queries, saturating shared CPU, so order-service INSERTs into orders queue and exceed their statement timeout. The autovacuum scale-factor change at 08:00Z is temporally separated (55+ min) from the 08:56Z load step and shows no vacuum-related blocking in logs.
